headline: OpenAI hit with sweeping probe from 42 US state attorneys general over ads, data, and minors
summary: A coalition of 42 US state attorneys general has launched a broad investigation into OpenAI, issuing a subpoena just days after its reported IPO filing. The probe targets the company's advertising, data practices, and handling of minors.
details: A coalition of 42 US state attorneys general has launched a sweeping investigation into OpenAI, issuing a broad subpoena on June 12. Led by New York AG Letitia James, the probe seeks documents on the company's advertising, user engagement, and data handling.

The investigation also focuses on OpenAI's activities involving minors and seniors, its use of deep learning models, model sycophancy, and internal company policies. OpenAI stated it takes these concerns seriously and intends to engage constructively with the offices.

This probe comes just five days after OpenAI confidentially filed paperwork for an IPO, reportedly valuing the company at up to $1 trillion. While an information-gathering step, its breadth suggests regulators are examining both business practices and AI safety risks.

OpenAI is already facing other legal challenges, including a civil lawsuit filed by Florida's Attorney General on June 1. Florida accuses OpenAI of knowingly releasing ChatGPT to the public, including children, while allegedly concealing serious risks and suppressing internal safety warnings.

The Florida complaint claims the chatbot can facilitate harm, including self-harm and violence, and alleges data collection from minors without proper parental oversight. The recent subpoena also highlights concerns about OpenAI's handling of sensitive consumer and health data shared with chatbots.

The investigation reflects a broader regulatory reckoning for AI technology, which has scaled rapidly ahead of established legal frameworks. OpenAI has committed to cooperating with the attorneys general as the information-gathering exercise proceeds.

headline: Microsoft is reportedly testing Copilot+ AI features with discrete GPUs instead of NPUs
summary: Microsoft is reportedly expanding Copilot+ AI features to work with discrete GPUs like Nvidia RTX 30-series, potentially freeing users from NPU-exclusive requirements. This move could bring local AI to millions of existing Windows PCs.
details: Microsoft is reportedly testing Copilot+ AI features to run on discrete GPUs, moving beyond the NPU-exclusive requirement. This experimental capability is available via a Windows App SDK build, requiring a Windows Insider Experimental Channel and Developer Mode.

The feature currently supports Nvidia GeForce RTX 30-series cards with at least 6GB of VRAM. While not all Copilot+ PC features will be available, it signals a broader approach to local AI inferencing on Windows.

This development is good news for millions of users whose current PCs lack a built-in NPU, allowing them access to some Copilot features. It also extends Windows' AI capabilities to desktop users, who typically don't have NPU-equipped processors.

NPUs are valued for efficiency in laptops, but GPUs can be more powerful for AI processing. Microsoft's shift may be influenced by lower-than-expected AI PC adoption and rising memory prices affecting new PC sales.

By expanding Copilot+ features to non-NPU devices, Microsoft aims to increase its user base and differentiate Windows 11. This strategy could help counter the impact of declining PC sales and growing competition from macOS and Linux.
